title: Non-equilibrium theory of projected ensembles
abstract: Projected ensembles---the collections of conditional pure states induced on a system by measuring an entangled environment---have become central objects in quantum science, underlying deep thermalization, quantum state designs, the emergence of classicality, and exhibiting interesting phase transitions. Here we develop a general and exact theory of their dynamics, yielding a systematic approach to their dynamics and equilibrium and non-equilibrium stationary states. We derive an exact continuity equation on quantum state space for the projected ensemble, together with microscopic kinetic equations and analytical expressions for the probability flux and source terms generated by the system-environment interaction. The resulting dynamics admits a classical representation: isolated systems obey Hamiltonian transport and Liouville's theorem, while open systems are described by a kinetic theory of probability transport. The stationary continuity equation provides a general characterization of equilibrium and non-equilibrium stationary projected ensembles, which can be analyzed through the method of characteristics. The theory provides an analytical framework for studying the emergence, structure, and timescales of equilibrium and non-equilibrium stationary projected ensembles, with applications ranging from deep thermalization and the emergence of classicality to random quantum-state generation and quantum device benchmarking.
summary: This paper establishes an exact theoretical framework for describing the dynamics of projected ensembles, which characterize how a system's state evolves after interacting with an environment. The core result is a continuity equation governing probability flow across the quantum state space. This allows researchers to analyze complex non-equilibrium steady states in systems ranging from qubits to many-body models.
main_problem: To develop a general and exact theory for the dynamics of projected ensembles, which are collections of conditional pure states induced by measuring an entangled environment.
main_result:
The theory yields an exact continuity equation on quantum state space ($\dot{\mu}_t + 
abla \cdot J_t = \sigma_t$), providing a framework to characterize both equilibrium and non-equilibrium stationary projected ensembles.
method: The dynamics are formulated as a problem of probability transport on the manifold of pure states, utilizing the symplectic structure of quantum state space and employing the method of characteristics for analysis.
model_or_system: The theory applies to open quantum systems undergoing system-environment interaction. Specific examples include analyzing projected ensembles in spin-star models or deriving Fokker-Planck equations for qubits on $	ext{CP}^1$.
key_observables: Projected ensemble ($\mu$ or $q(z)$), probability flux ($J_t$), and source/sink terms ($\sigma_t$).
important_parameters: The system-environment coupling strength, temperature (implicitly via equilibrium analysis), and the dimensionality of the Hilbert space.
main_assumptions: The theory is general and exact, relying on exploiting the symplectic structure of $	ext{P}(H)$. Specific derivations assume bipartite decomposition or specific noise/drift structures for simplified models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a geometric quantum state representation on the Bloch sphere. Figure 4 compares numerically calculated time-averaged projected ensembles against analytically derived stationary states for the spin-star model, showing excellent agreement.
paper_structure:
The paper develops the theory by first establishing the general continuity equation ($\dot{\mu}_t + 
abla \cdot J_t = \sigma_t$), then detailing how this governs probability transport via flux ($J_t$) and source/sink terms ($\sigma_t$). It applies this framework to specific models, such as the spin-star model or qubit dynamics on $	ext{CP}^1$, to derive concrete stationary state solutions.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general mathematical machinery—the continuity equation approach—to study non-equilibrium steady states in open quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding thermalization and quantum measurement processes beyond simple Markovian master equations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An example of a geometric quantum state for a qubit, D = 2. Each point is one element Γα of the ensemble, carrying a probability mass xα (color scale). Left: A representation of the ensemble on the Bloch sphere. Right: the same ensemble in canonically conjugated probability-phase coordinates, in which the state of the qubit is parameterized as |ψ⟩= √1 −p |0⟩+ √p eiϕ |1⟩and the state space becomes the “Bloch square” [0, 1] × [0, 2π), with the poles p = 0, 1 mapping to its lower and upper edges.

Figure 2: A diagrammatic view of the continuity equtaion. Left: Kinetic interpretation of the probability flux Jt. If we look at a small region of the quantum state space, due to the underlying dynamics we see that probability is locally conserved in the sense that there is a certain number of points which enters and leaves this region. As a result of this local process, probability is moved around and can concentrate in a certain region or get scrambled across the quantum state space. Right: Kinetic interpretation of the sink/source term σt. Figure 3: Left: Relaxation of a single stochastic trajectory of the qubit–Caldeira–Leggett Langevin equations, Eq. (13), toward the geometric canonical ensemble. Each panel shows the time-averaged histogram of (p, ϕ) accumulated over the trajectory up to the indicated step, exploiting the ergodicity of the process to approximate the ensemble qt from a single realization of the noise rather than an average over many. Starting from a narrow initial distribution, the trajectory is driven by the Hamiltonian drift toward the pole p = 1 before the dissipative and diffusive terms relax it onto a stationary profile. The central spin is initialized in |0⟩and the bath is prepared at mean magnetization m0 = 0.5. Weights are shown on a logarithmic color scale.
